Paragraph:
Translation: All created beings are unmanifest in their beginning, manifest in their interim state, and unmanifest again when they are annihilated. So what need is there for lamentation?

Purport (Excerpt): Apart from the separate existence of the soul, the material elements remain unmanifested before creation... Both at the beginning and at the end, all elements remain unmanifested, and only in the middle are they manifested, and this does not make any real material difference... The material body has no factual existence in relation to the eternal soul. It is something like a dream.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Arjuna is overly attached to the physical presence (manifest state) of his loved ones.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Krishna provides a macro-perspective of existence. He explains that bodies are just temporary manifestations of elements. Before birth, they were invisible (unmanifest). After death, they return to being invisible (unmanifest). The brief period of visibility (life) is just a temporary middle phase.
Outcome/Resolution: By zooming out, the current physical reality is minimized to a fleeting dream, reducing the emotional sting of its loss.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.macro-Perspective: Looking at the big picture of time
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.detachment: Letting go of the need for things to stay the same

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Avyakta (The unmanifested state of material energy)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Material bodies are simply temporary configurations of eternal elements. They come from the unmanifest, briefly appear as forms, and return to the unmanifest. Recognizing that the 'manifest' stage is transient and ultimately dream-like compared to eternal spirit helps dissolve worldly attachments.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Krishna uses a powerful reframing technique: temporal distancing. When someone is anxious, they are hyper-focused on the immediate present. By forcing Arjuna to look at the 'before' and the 'after' (which are both states of non-existence for the physical body), the 'present' moment loses its overwhelming, absolute power.
